name: South Carolina

notes: Unprepared food (what SNAP can buy, candy and soft drinks included) is exempt from the 6% state tax; of the local taxes, the local option tax and most transportation taxes apply to it and the capital projects, education and school district taxes don't, so the local rate on groceries here is each county's own from SCDOR's ST-575 (0% to 2%). Prepared food is taxed at the full rate plus local hospitality taxes.
Alcohol bought in stores is taxed at the full rate.
Drinks served pay the sales tax; drinks with liquor also pay the 5% liquor-by-the-drink tax, counted here on drinks with distilled spirits, 43% of drinks served nationally (2022 Economic Census).

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the full rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: 57 cents a pack of cigarettes, 5% of the manufacturer's price on other tobacco and 5 cents a milliliter of vapor liquid.
Personal care products: feminine hygiene products are exempt (since 2024, SC Code 12-36-2120(84)), which is not taken out here; diapers are taxed.
Barber and beauty services, and auto repair labor: not taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).
Clothing is taxed. The back-to-school sales tax holiday (August 7 to 9, 2026) exempted clothing, shoes and school supplies from state and SCDOR-collected local taxes, which is not taken out here.
Laundry and dry cleaning: taxed (FTA 2017 survey answer).
Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and pays a 28-cent-a-gallon user fee instead (since July 1, 2022), left out here.
People 85 or older pay 1% less state sales tax on purchases for their own use (SC Revenue Ruling 16-9), which is not taken out here.

Hotel stays pay the 7% state accommodations tax (the 5% sales tax plus 2%), local accommodations taxes up to 3% and SCDOR-collected local taxes (Charleston's total is 14%), which are not counted here.

A 2026 law (Act 228, the Municipal Tax Relief Act) lets cities levy their own sales tax of up to 1%, groceries exempt, after a vote; nine cities vote on one on November 3, 2026 (Greenville, Mauldin, Simpsonville, Travelers Rest, Seneca, Walhalla, Westminster, Salem and West Union), which would start May 1, 2027 at the earliest. The current rates are used here.
gaps: South Carolina rates are SCDOR's county totals for May 1, 2026 and after; every municipality takes its county's rate except Myrtle Beach (SCDOR's ST-575, "Sales Tax Rate by Municipality"). The Catawba Indian Nation's tax equals York County's rate (Information Letter #26-5).
The local rate on groceries is each county's own from SCDOR's ST-575: capital projects, education, school district and some transportation taxes don't apply to food.
Municipal Tourism Development tax is added only for Myrtle Beach, the municipality SCDOR lists for it in Information Letter #26-5.
South Carolina caps the tax on some big-ticket items (maximum tax items); not relevant to the categories here.

Hospitality taxes on prepared food and drinks (up to 2%, collected by cities and counties, not SCDOR) are counted in restaurant rates for 117 cities and towns and, outside their cities, 24 counties: from the government's own page where found, otherwise from the Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office's tables of local hospitality taxes (fiscal year 2023-24, as reported by each government). 14 more report hospitality tax revenue but no rate; they are noted, not counted. A county's tax inside its cities is counted only where the county says so: Horry's 1.5% in every city, Clarendon's 1% throughout the county, and Colleton's in 5 towns, Dorchester's in 2 towns, Florence's in 3 towns, Georgetown's in 1 town, Lee's in 1 town, Richland's in 2 towns, Spartanburg's in 1 town, Sumter's in 2 towns, Williamsburg's in 4 towns and York's in 4 towns. Where a county's form also lists a town that reports its own tax, the higher rate is counted, not both.
Sales tax votes on November 3, 2026 in 14 counties are noted on those pages, with the current rates used; none would take effect before April 2027.

tiers.label: South Carolina job tax credit tier
tiers.what: Sets the per-job corporate income tax credit for new full-time jobs created in tax years beginning in 2026; the credit per job rises from Tier I (most developed) to Tier IV (least developed), with amounts set in S.C. Code §12-6-3360.

programs: Tax increment financing districts are mapped for Charleston only: Rock Hill's (a York County layer from 2020 with no status) and Sumter's (2014) layers aren't current enough to use, and Columbia, Greenville, North Charleston, Spartanburg, Myrtle Beach and Mount Pleasant publish none. The state's incentives are tax credits by county tier (shown with the tiers) rather than zones. Main Street South Carolina's communities aren't shown: the Municipal Association lists 34 (4 accredited, 12 classic and 18 in its Friends tier, a membership level rather than a designation) and publishes no map.

warn: Edisto Beach's page is built from the one census tract that lies at least half inside the town, which is almost all water and has no residents, so it shows no resident spending; the town's homes are in the neighboring tract (Colleton County 9708, shown under Jacksonboro), which is flagged as a visitor economy.

warn.text: Charleston draws many visitors (its historic district and nearby beaches), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (3.4%) and its 154 lodging places (1.1 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs over the city as a whole, though 9 of its 34 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Brookdale may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its hotels and motels along the interstate (21 lodging places, 5.5 per 1,000 residents), serving travelers passing through, so read that flag with care.
